content: Induction of labor is a frequently performed procedure in obstetrics. The combination of amniotomy and intravenous oxytocin for inducing labor in the third trimester has been specifically reviewed in this study. This review is part of a broader series examining various methods of cervical ripening and labor induction using standardized methodologies. The primary objective of this review was to evaluate the efficacy and safety of combining amniotomy with intravenous oxytocin for labor induction in the third trimester, based on the best available evidence. To gather relevant data, the researchers conducted a comprehensive search of the Cochrane Pregnancy and Childbirth Group's Trials Register, the Cochrane Controlled Trials Register, and reference lists of related articles. The last search was conducted in May 2001, with an updated search performed on September 21, 2009. The results of the updated search were added to the awaiting classification section of the review. The review included clinical trials that compared the combination of amniotomy and intravenous oxytocin with either placebo, no treatment, or other predefined methods of labor induction. The quality of the trials and the data were assessed and extracted by two reviewers. A two-stage data extraction process was employed due to the complexity and volume of the data. Initially, data were extracted centrally and incorporated into primary reviews organized by induction methods. Subsequently, the data were further categorized into secondary reviews based on the characteristics of the women involved. Seventeen trials involving a total of 2,566 women were included in the analysis. The combination of amniotomy and intravenous oxytocin was associated with a lower likelihood of women remaining undelivered vaginally at 24 hours compared to amniotomy alone (relative risk [RR] 0.03, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.001–0.49). However, this finding was based on a single study involving 100 women. In terms of secondary outcomes, the combination of amniotomy and intravenous oxytocin resulted in significantly fewer instrumental vaginal deliveries compared to placebo (RR 0.18, CI 0.05–0.58). However, this combination was associated with a higher incidence of postpartum hemorrhage compared to vaginal prostaglandins (RR 5.5, CI 1.26–24.07). Additionally, women reported significantly higher dissatisfaction with the combination of amniotomy and intravenous oxytocin compared to vaginal prostaglandins (RR 53, CI 3.32–846.51). The authors concluded that there is insufficient data on the effectiveness and safety of combining amniotomy with intravenous oxytocin for labor induction. As a result, no definitive recommendations for clinical practice can be made based on this review. While both methods are commonly used in clinical settings, further research is necessary to compare their effectiveness and safety and to determine the specific clinical scenarios in which one method may be preferable over the other. It is also noted that three citations in the awaiting classification section of the review may potentially alter the conclusions once they are assessed.
